title: Stephen Miller replaces Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
description: White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is being replaced by Stephen Miller, President Trump said Friday. The change comes after Republicans wer
body:
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles is being replaced by Stephen Miller, President Trump said Friday. The change comes after Republicans were swept out of power in the midterm elections.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  President Trump has announced that he is replacing Susie Wiles as chief of staff with Stephen Miller, who's behind some of Trump's most controversial policies.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: Stephen's been with me from beginning. He gets it.CHANG: Now, this is a major shake-up just days after Republicans' historic losses in this year's midterm elections. And it's a sign that the White House is not ready to back down from its agenda after those losses. NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben joins us now to explain. Hi, Danielle.DANIELLE KURTZLEBEN, BYLINE: Hey there.CHANG: OK, so what do we know so far about why Trump is even making this change? Like, do you think it has to do with the election?KURTZLEBEN: Well, let me start with how he announced it. He announced it in the way he announces a lot of things, in a social media post. And he said Miller will take over on Monday. Now Trump also said that Wiles, who is the nation's first female White House chief of staff, that she's done an outstanding job and that she's moving to his political operation. Now, the prospect of a shake-up had come up recently, even before the midterms. There were reports that Trump was then considering replacing her. Now, today, as Trump departed the White House for Florida, he didn't have a lot in the way of explanation. He said, quote, "sometimes in life, you have to make moves." So not much there.CHANG: OK.KURTZLEBEN: But whatever his reasons, it sends a loud message after Tuesday of not backing down on some of their most aggressive policies.CHANG: Yeah. OK, let's say more about that message. What should we know about Stephen Miller in this new, arguably more powerful, role?KURTZLEBEN: Well, you could read these losses as a clear repudiation of Trump's policies, but then Miller is a true MAGA believer. I mean, he's been with the president since his 2016 campaign. He's always been considered one of the chief architects in particular of the president's hard-line immigration policies. So this seems to be the administration saying, full speed ahead. Now Miller, after all, he's known as an aggressive defender of Trump, also an aggressive mouthpiece. Here he was defending the idea of the U.S. taking over Greenland on CNN earlier this year.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)STEPHEN MILLER: The real question is, by what right does Denmark assert control over Greenland? What is the basis of their territorial claim? What is their basis of having Greenland as a colony of Denmark? The United States is the power of NATO.KURTZLEBEN: So really pushing one of the administration's more aggressive policies there.CHANG: Yeah.KURTZLEBEN: And also, though, this highlights one more thing - that the new Congress may well constrain this White House, but the president does have a lot of foreign policy power, and now Miller and his foreign policy ideas will now be elevated.CHANG: Indeed. Can you talk more about what we know about what Wiles was like? Like, how big of a change might Miller be from Wiles?KURTZLEBEN: Well Wiles was known to be a savvy political operator. She saw her job as Trump's top aid to make recommendations, but not necessarily to tell the president no. Here she was talking about her role on the Mom View podcast.(SOUNDBITE OF PODCAST, "MOM VIEW")SUSIE WILES: We've been together a long time, and I'm so lucky every day that he trusts me to make decisions and to make recommendations. He doesn't always listen or do what I say. I don't want him to. But I'm always heard, and that's all you can ask.UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: That's right.KURTZLEBEN: Now Miller, on the other hand, is more like someone who is going to pour rocket fuel on Trump's desires. He was an aid to Alabama Senator Jeff Sessions, who became Trump's first attorney general, and Miller also has a reputation as a policy wonk willing to try new and inventive ways to expand Trump's power.CHANG: So what's been the initial reaction to this announcement?KURTZLEBEN: Well, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who's soon expected to be the new House speaker, posted this on social media. Quote, "Stephen Miller is a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands. His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today." So that's about as direct as it gets.CHANG: Yeah.KURTZLEBEN: And you might remember that Trump said this week that he could maybe compromise with a Democratic Congress, and chiefs of staff often do keep relationships open with all factions. Well, the Miller pick doesn't signal that that's a priority, and the feeling seems mutual from Jeffries.CHANG: That is NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben. Thank you, Danielle.KURTZLEBEN: Of course.

title: American democracy was a big winner in the midterms
description: Results are still outstanding House and Senate races but political scientists say one of the big winners in the mid-terms is American democracy
body:
Results are still outstanding House and Senate races but political scientists say one of the big winners in the mid-terms is American democracy itself.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  Four days on, some House and Senate races have yet to be called. But political scientists say that one of the big, clear winners of the midterms is American democracy itself. NPR's Frank Langfitt reports.FRANK LANGFITT, BYLINE: Bright Line Watch is a national survey that asks hundreds of political scientists about the health of American democracy. After Trump took office last year, most scholars saw the U.S. moving swiftly towards some form of authoritarianism. With the president talking up fears of election fraud ahead of the midterms, Bright Line's co-director Brendan Nyhan says there was a lot of concern.BRENDAN NYHAN: In our pre-election survey of political science experts, it was widely expected that prominent Republicans would deny the legitimacy of the election results.LANGFITT: As we now know, that didn't happen.NYHAN: I think the clarity of the result just made it hard to deny. People have this phrase - too big to rig.LANGFITT: And President Trump, who lied about losing the 2020 election, said he'd accept these results.NYHAN: It's a remarkable turning point. We've been in the age of Trump for 10 years. The threat to democracy has been acute. It wasn't clear whether he'd be able to subvert this election, but the system held.LANGFITT: NPR reached out to the White House. Spokeswoman Lauren Biss responded by calling this report, quote, "another completely ridiculous news story by NPR and a perfect example of why the president stopped American taxpayers from subsidizing this fake news outlet. President Trump has done more than any other president to ensure we have free and fair elections." In fact, Steven Levitsky, a professor of government at Harvard, says the Trump administration tried lots of things to give Republicans an advantage in the midterms.STEVEN LEVITSKY: It has thrown two dozen pieces of spaghetti at the wall in the form of trying to centralize voter lists and trying to stop or subvert vote by mail. It engaged in an unprecedented national gerrymandering scheme to try to tilt the electoral balance in the house. None of that worked.LANGFITT: Levitsky credits lawyers who mounted legal challenges and the courts, which often blocked Trump's moves.LEVITSKY: Critics of the Trump administration, the opposition, Democratic Party, civil society was much more aware of the threat to democracy and was very, very active in combating it.LANGFITT: Lorinc Redei grew up in Hungary and is a professor at the University of Texas at Austin. He says the Republican defeat fits a pattern in Europe this year, where ruling parties with autocratic leaders were toppled after failing to address kitchen table issues.LORINC REDEI: In Hungary, you had falling living standards, high inflation, terrible hospital conditions. Those were the things that brought people out to vote. In Serbia recently, you had failing infrastructure and high unemployment. That's what people were upset about.LANGFITT: Redei says there's a lesson here.REDEI: Elections still matter. If there's enough significant public outcry against the government and they go vote, you lose elections.LANGFITT: None of the scholars NPR spoke with think the threats to American democracy are over. Nyhan, a professor at Dartmouth, points out that the blue wave was not driven by political ideals.NYHAN: To the extent that we can tell, it's far more a repudiation of Donald Trump's management of the economy and the war in Iran, for instance, than it is a repudiation of his attack on democracy.LANGFITT: Here's Steven Levitsky of Harvard.LEVITSKY: I see no reason why Trump won't continue to try to engage in authoritarian shenanigans. I think he'll probably be less successful, one, because he's weaker, two, because the Democrats control Congress and will have some levers that they can pull to constrain him.LANGFITT: And three, Levitsky thinks - some Republicans, for the first time, will begin to defect from the president.Frank Langfitt, NPR News, Washington.(SOUNDBITE OF ELMIENE AND BADBADNOTGOOD SONG, "MARKING MY TIME")

title: What to know about Gina Hinojosa, Texas' first Latina governor-elect
description: Gina Hinojosa, state representative from the Rio Grande Valley whose legislative priority has been boosting the public education system, will b
body:
Gina Hinojosa, state representative from the Rio Grande Valley whose legislative priority has been boosting the public education system, will become the first Latina governor of Texas.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    AILSA CHANG, HOST:  Among many big wins for Democrats in this week's midterms was the race for governor of Texas. Democrat Gina Hinojosa's victory will end three decades of Republican control of the state's top office. The former school board president is now preparing to lead Texas as its first Latina governor. From The Texas Newsroom, Blaise Gainey reports.BLAISE GAINEY, BYLINE: On election night, as she stood with her husband and two sons, Gina Hinojosa traced her path to the governor's mansion back to 2011, when her son's school in Austin, Pease Elementary, was under threat of closing.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)GINA HINOJOSA: And when I saw my child's school under threat, I did what any mom would do. I fought back.(CHEERING)GAINEY: In 2012, she was elected to Austin's school board. She wanted more say in the decisions about the education of the community's children. A product of public schools herself, Hinojosa became a civil rights and labor lawyer. She grew up in Brownsville, Texas, a border town in the Rio Grande Valley. Democratic State Representative John Bucy says that concern for children has followed her to the Capitol.JOHN BUCY: She's going to be fighting for the kids of this state. She did it on the school board. She's done it every day in the legislature.GAINEY: Fighting back was a core message in her campaign.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)HINOJOSA: I can't help but think of my grandmother, Grandma Hinojosa...(CHEERING)HINOJOSA: ...Who used to tell me, no te dejes.(CHEERING)HINOJOSA: Know your worth, and fight to defend it.GAINEY: Her old colleague in the House, Democratic State Representative Trey Martinez Fischer, called Hinojosa a tactician for her ability to strategize to reach her goals. In 2023, instead of having Democrats lead the debate against private school vouchers, she convinced her party to let rural Republicans lead the opposition. And then last year, she was part of a group of Democratic legislators who fled the state to try to stall Republicans' attempt to redraw congressional districts in their favor. She explained her reasoning to NPR from Chicago.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)HINOJOSA: You win for the day. And we don't know what tomorrow will hold, so it's a day-by-day situational fight, and we'll play to win every day.GAINEY: The Republican majority eventually approved that map. Now Hinojosa faces the work of governing after Tuesday's election, where Democrats won by a landslide in all the statewide races. On Thursday, during her first press conference since becoming governor-elect, Hinojosa said she'd be working for all Texans, highlighting her bipartisan approach by choosing a Republican, former state representative Ernest Bailes, to be on her transition team.(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)HINOJOSA: People are tired of the divisions, of the fighting, tired of the culture wars. This is a time to come together in a way that is about just delivering for the people of Texas.GAINEY: The victory carries a personal meaning for comedian Cristela Alonzo. She campaigned for Hinojosa in the Rio Grande Valley, where they both grew up. As a child, Alonzo said she wanted to be president but was told a poor girl from the Valley couldn't do that. At a rally at University of Texas Rio Grande Valley just days before the election, Alonzo told students Hinojosa's success meant they could do it, too.CRISTELA ALONZO: And now they actually have an example of seeing someone and say, you can be governor? And that is possible because of her. If you can be governor, what more can you be?GAINEY: On January 19, Hinojosa, who calls herself a daughter of the Rio Grande Valley, will become the top elected official of the Lone Star state.For NPR News, I'm Blaise Gainey.

title: An unexpected activist emerged to help block a $5 billion data center in Maryland
description: Taylor Frazier McCollum has been active
body:
Taylor Frazier McCollum has been active in the opposition to the possible data center at the site of the demolished Landover Mall in Prince George's County, less than a mile from where she lived. If the project is built, the development could occupy more than 80 acres.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   The overgrown grass and weeds seem to stretch into the horizon on nearly 90 acres of empty land in Landover, Md. It used to be Landover Mall, but that closed in 2002, and the site has been mostly vacant since.   In 2024, the developer that built the mall won approval from county planners for a $5 billion data center campus, and word began spreading through the largely Black community nearby.   "I was like, 'Oh, hell no,'" said Taylor Frazier McCollum, describing the moment she learned about the project. She lived less than a mile away from it. "Why would you want to bring water-polluting, diesel-generating data centers right down the street from where people live, work, play? It just didn't make sense to me."   
   Frazier McCollum is one of a number of Americans whose political awakening was triggered by data center development. Across the country, community members have taken to local council hearings to voice their opposition. They've prompted — though estimates vary — about 500 moratoriums on data centers nationwide.   A different kind of land-use activist   Unlike a lot of land-use activists trying to protect their homes from threats in their backyards, Frazier McCollum does not own a home. In 2024, she and her young daughter were evicted from their apartment. She was working at a waxing center that cut wages, and she could no longer cover her rent.   "It was difficult," Frazier McCollum recalled. "Because I created the ideal life paying for us to live in this apartment and have our own space ... and then to have it taken away ... It felt like something that wasn't ever going to end."   They've moved around and were living in her grandfather's home when she learned about the proposed project less than a mile away.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Taylor Frazier McCollum in front of her grandfather's home, where she lived when she heard about the proposed data center site less than a mile away in Landover, Md.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   She created a petition that gathered over 25,000 signatures, leading to widely attended protests and culminating in multiple local moratoriums imposed on data centers throughout the county. It blocked the $5 billion project that was set to break ground between 2026 and 2027.   
   The fight pushed Frazier McCollum to the forefront of local politics. She went to county meetings, testified before Maryland legislators and endorsed political candidates. She found herself in a coalition of socialists, environmentalists, people angry about their electric bills and neighbors new to organizing.   Local media interviewed her, and people in data center circles called her "the Landover girl."   After some losses, the county needs revenue, and data centers could help   Staci Hartwell, a longtime local environmental activist, says she spent years struggling to get traction on the data center issue before Frazier McCollum came along.   "This is something that was happening in her neighborhood, and it was really like her awakening," Hartwell said.   But with data centers paused, some in Prince George's County worry about declining tax revenue. Last year, a local Six Flags closed. The NFL's Washington Commanders announced plans to return to neighboring Washington, D.C. Thousands of federal workers have lost their jobs. The county faces a budget deficit.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The possible data center site, which was once the Landover Mall, in Prince George's County. If the project is built, the development will occupy more than 80 acres.
                
                    Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
    

   
   In September, Frazier McCollum appeared at a county council meeting to advocate for a fund for roof repairs, something her grandfather's home needs. Council member Wanika Fisher, who supports moving some data center projects forward, reminded her that the county needs development.   "Our county has an economic future that we have to grapple with," said Fisher, addressing the request. "I don't see where the money is coming from. I think we have to have a real conversation. And I'm not saying that a data center is the answer, but I'm saying it's worth the hard discussion."   Now Frazier McCollum is broadening her activism and going to new places   With the Landover project on hold, Frazier McCollum now wants a full ban on that and other data center projects. And with grants Hartwell and others have found, Frazier McCollum has taken her message to Black communities fighting data center growth in Atlanta, Memphis and even across the globe in Zambia.   
   "I feel like so many people are depending on this fight to be successful," Frazier McCollum explained. "Not just for myself, but even across the country, to set precedent for other people that are fighting against hyperscale data centers."   She's lost out on work to attend public meetings or knock on doors, and she's relied on family for rides and childcare.   Her father, Lacy McCollum Jr., sees the data center fight as rooted in civil rights.   
   "We're talking about the right to water, the right to clean air, the right to a place to live. That's everybody's fight, right?" Lacy McCollum Jr. said. "While I'm afraid for her, we need those people. We needed the Medgar Everses. We needed the Martin Luther Kings. We needed the Malcolm X's. People like Taylor, they jump out here so the people behind them get to make progress."   Some urge her to run for office. She says she wants to pay off her debt and traffic tickets and find a home first.   "I didn't want to have to focus on housing and the campaign and doing everything else," explained Frazier McCollum. "Now is not maybe the moment for it, but I do have aspirations to run for something."   In the meantime, she's pitching plans to turn the old Landover site into a sports complex or affordable housing, or to use some of it to support heritage tourism in the county. But none of those ideas, she acknowledges, would be as lucrative as a data center campus.      Jenny Abamu is a reporter for WAMU.
